title: Deciding finite-lattice embeddability into c.e. degrees
formal: Is there an algorithm deciding whether a finite lattice embeds into R preserving binary joins and meets?
definitions: A set A of natural numbers is computably enumerable (c.e.) if a finite ordinary Turing program enumerates exactly A. Write A≤_T B when an oracle Turing machine with membership access to B decides membership in A on every input. Equivalence under mutual reducibility defines a Turing degree. R is the set of degrees containing a c.e. set, ordered by ≤_T; it is not the set of all degrees below the halting problem. All quantification over degrees below is over R. The language has only ≤ and logical equality, with no named degrees or parameters unless explicitly stated. Input consists of a positive integer m and two m×m operation tables on {0,…,m−1}, encoded in binary, promised to define a lattice L. An embedding is an injective map f:L→R such that f(a∨b) is the least upper bound of f(a),f(b) in R and f(a∧b) is their greatest lower bound in R, for every a,b∈L. The latter bound must be above every common lower bound: each degree d≤f(a),f(b) satisfies d≤f(a∧b). There is no requirement that f(0_L) be the computable degree or that f(1_L) be the halting degree. This is explicitly the unbounded-lattice embedding convention. A decider must halt and answer correctly on every promised input; no running-time bound or output of an embedding is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation, with exactly the structures and quantifiers specified here. Decidability only for a restricted family of finite lattices does not suffice.
context: The survey asks whether embeddable finite lattices form a computable class, and separates restricted meet patterns from the full problem.
why: This asks for an effective description of the finite algebraic patterns realizable by relative computability.

sentences: A finite lattice is given by its join and meet tables.
An embedding must preserve both operations in the c.e. degree structure.
Meets must be genuine greatest lower bounds among all c.e. degrees.
The least and greatest input elements need not map to the global bounds.
The target is a decision algorithm for all finite lattices.
